LLM_description:
Situation:
Task Force Iron is conducting sustained operations across AO Falcon. Supported elements are dispersed among forward operating bases and patrol bases with limited organic lift. Supply Depot Bravo in the rear and Forward Supply Point Delta closer to the line hold the critical stock. Main supply routes traverse a river valley, urban outskirts, and a mountain pass. Weather and enemy activity intermittently degrade road conditions; route clearance assets are limited and escorts must be scheduled. Some units are within indirect fire threat envelopes, complicating convoy timings and halts. Movement control must balance route security, depot throughput, and fleet availability over the planning horizon.

Mission:
Deliver the required supply to designated units from available depots while minimizing total operational cost (transport, shortage penalties, vehicle deployment, and fixed route security risk costs), maintaining unit combat effectiveness, and preserving fleet readiness.

Execution/Concept:
- Distribution will allocate flows from each depot to each supported unit by day, respecting depot daily capacity and unit demand. Controlled shortfalls are permitted when operationally acceptable and will incur shortage penalties.
- Vehicle capacity constraints govern how much supply can be lifted per movement; flows must be matched to available trucks on each depot-to-unit route per day.
- Routes can only be used once they are activated. Activating a route (sending any vehicles on that path for that day) incurs a fixed Risk Cost representing security overhead—escort teams, route clearance, overwatch—regardless of the number of vehicles deployed on that route.
- Total fleet employment across all routes per day is limited; vehicles cannot exceed fleet availability. Convoy assignments are integer values aligned to movement control practices.
- Transport costs vary by depot-to-unit pairing and reflect distance, terrain, and threat. Risk costs reflect the security package required to open and hold the route. Penalty costs quantify the operational impact of unmet demand.
- Priority of effort will favor units in contact and critical enablers. Where risk or capacity constraints preclude simultaneous support to all, we will consolidate movements on the most secure routes, shift loads between depots, and stagger deliveries across days to meet the mission at minimum cost.
- Coordination with engineers, military police, and aviation overwatch will be synchronized to route activation windows. Movement control will sequence convoys to avoid route overlap and choke points while preserving depot throughput.

LLM_description_template:
Situation:
The brigade is sustaining dispersed combat elements across a contested corridor. Shipments will move from Supply Depot Bravo and Logistics Hub Delta to forward units—Infantry Battalion Echo, Cavalry Squadron Hawk, Engineer Company Foxtrot, Artillery Battery Lion, Reconnaissance Troop Raven, and Medical Company Sierra—over a short, time-phased window. Ground movement is constrained by enemy activity along lowland routes, periodic interdiction of key bridges, and weather impacts on high-ground passes. Route clearance assets and escorts are limited; activating any ground corridor requires task-organized security, EOD teams, ISR coverage, and a quick-reaction force on standby.

Mission:
Deliver the designated sustainment commodity from rear-area depots to all supported units across the planning horizon while minimizing total operational cost. Costs include per-unit transport, fixed route security risk charges for each corridor placed into operation, per-vehicle deployment costs, and penalties for any shortfall in unit requirements.

Execution/Concept:
- Distribution framework: Direct ground shipments from each depot to each unit by day. No transshipment or cross-docking en route. All flows are time-phased and must align with depot on-hand stocks and route availability.
- Risk and route activation: Activating any route on a given day—defined as assigning one or more vehicles to that corridor—incurs a fixed Risk Cost that covers escorts, route clearance, ISR, and QRF, regardless of the number of vehicles dispatched. This fixed overhead applies each day a corridor is active and is independent of shipment volume.
- Transport economics: Per-route transport costs reflect distance, terrain, and expected delays. Vehicle deployment costs account for fuel, maintenance, and crew tempo. The optimization will weigh higher transport rates against the fixed risk overhead of opening additional corridors.
- Supply and demand discipline: 
  - Depot capacity: Daily shipments from a depot cannot exceed its available, time-phased stock.
  - Unit demand: Each unit’s requirement is enforced daily. Controlled shortfalls are captured as slack and incur a penalty to represent readiness and operational risk.
- Mobility constraints:
  - Vehicle capacity: Shipment volume consumes vehicle capacity per the commodity’s bulk/weight factor; assigned vehicles bound the maximum throughput on any route-day.
  - Route gating: Vehicles can only be assigned to corridors that have been activated; non-activated routes cannot carry traffic.
  - Fleet ceiling: Total vehicles employed across all routes on a given day cannot exceed the available fleet.
- Prioritization and phasing: Emphasis is placed on early movement to units with critical readiness demands and exposed positions. When routes through the valley are under observation or high IED risk, the plan favors fewer, better-protected corridors with higher load factors to reduce fixed security overhead.
- Decision logic: The distribution plan will:
  - Select the minimum set of route activations required to meet operational priorities while limiting fixed Risk Cost outlays.
  - Allocate vehicles across active routes to maximize payload utilization within capacity constraints.
  - Balance depot drawdowns against future-day requirements.
  - Apply shortage penalties only where risk or cost makes immediate fulfillment infeasible.
